opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to where the workloads are and where I think I can have the most leverage.

For a long time the answer was pretty simple: NVIDIA. That's where almost all the training and inference was happening, the tooling was the most mature, and if you wrote a fast kernel there, it immediately mattered to a huge number of people. So a lot of the FlashAttention work started there and stayed there for a while.

But I try to think about it in terms of a few questions. First, is there real demand? Are people actually running large models on this hardware, or planning to soon? If there are going to be serious deployments, then the software gap becomes the bottleneck, and that's where someone like me can help.

Second, how different is the hardware, and is the difference interesting? Each new generation, even within one vendor, changes things. New tensor core instructions, asynchronous memory movement, different memory hierarchies. Sometimes the algorithm you designed for one chip is just wrong for the next one, and you have to rethink it. Those are the most fun problems, because you learn something general about how to map these workloads onto hardware.

Third, what's the state of the software stack? If the compilers and libraries are really good, there's less for me to add. If it's early, there's a lot of low-hanging fruit, but it can also be painful to work with. So there's a tradeoff between impact and how much time you spend fighting tooling.

More and more, I care about the abstractions that make it easier to move across chips. Writing everything by hand for every architecture doesn't scale. If we can find the right primitives, things like tiles, data movement, and the core matmul and reduction patterns, and build tools around those, then porting to AMD or other accelerators becomes much more tractable. That's partly why I'm excited about higher-level kernel languages and DSLs. You can get most of the performance while not rewriting from scratch every time.

So it's a mix of following where the models are actually being run and choosing places where the hardware forces you to learn something new.

r001.rationale: The response says Dao considers whether the hardware differences are interesting and describes those problems as fun, making interesting work an explicit criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to two things: where the researchers and the workloads actually are, and where I think the hardware is going to be interesting over the next couple of years.

The first one is pretty pragmatic. Most of the people I work with, most of the open-source community, most of the labs training big models, are on NVIDIA. So if I write a kernel and it runs well on an H100 or a B200, it has immediate impact. People pick it up the same week. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable for research. You find out very quickly what's broken, what matters, what nobody cares about. When I started FlashAttention it was really just about making attention fast on the GPUs people had access to, and that's still the center of gravity.

The second thing is that I get a lot of value from understanding a new architecture deeply. Every chip makes different bets about memory hierarchy, about how much on-chip SRAM you have, about how data moves between compute units. Going from Ampere to Hopper to Blackwell, each generation changed how you have to think about the algorithm, not just the implementation. Hopper gave you asynchronous tensor core instructions and TMA, and you had to restructure the whole pipeline to take advantage of that. Blackwell changes it again. So I spend time on new chips partly because the hardware constraints are what generate the interesting algorithmic ideas. The algorithm and the hardware co-design each other.

For other ecosystems, like AMD or TPUs or some of the newer accelerator startups, I try to stay involved, but I'm honest with myself about bandwidth. I'd rather do one thing really well and make the ideas portable than do a shallow port to five platforms. A lot of what we learned from FlashAttention transferred to other hardware because the core idea, which is that you should respect the memory hierarchy and avoid materializing big intermediates, is not NVIDIA-specific. Other teams took it and reimplemented it for their chips, which is the best outcome. I don't have to be the one writing every kernel.

And then there's the software layer. Tools like Triton, and more recently some of the Python-first DSLs, are getting good enough that you can express a kernel once and have a reasonable chance of running it on more than one backend. That shifts how I think about it. If the abstraction layer handles the portability, I can spend my time on the parts that are genuinely hardware-specific and matter for performance, instead of rewriting the same thing in a different vendor's dialect.

So the short version is: I go where the users are, I go where the hardware is doing something new, and I try to keep the ideas general enough that they outlive any particular chip.

r001.rationale: The response says he spends time on new chips because their hardware constraints generate interesting algorithmic ideas, identifying interesting work as a criterion.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of where the users are and where there’s an interesting technical problem to solve. If you make something faster, how many people can actually use it? That pushes you toward ecosystems that already have a lot of adoption. But there’s also an opportunity with newer hardware, where the software hasn’t caught up and a better algorithm or kernel could make a big difference.

The other part is how quickly you can experiment. Can you get access to the hardware? Are the tools good enough to understand why something is slow? Can you work with people who understand the architecture? You’re investing your time in that whole feedback loop, not just in the chip’s theoretical performance.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he considers where there is “an interesting technical problem to solve,” identifying interesting work as a criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about where the users are and where we can have the most impact. A lot of the work we do is making algorithms run efficiently on the hardware people already have. So the software ecosystem matters a lot: can we program the chip, profile it, and understand why something is slow? And if we build something useful, how many people can actually use it?

There’s also the question of whether the hardware gives us an interesting opportunity to rethink the algorithm. I like that interaction—you try to implement something, discover a bottleneck, and then ask whether you can change the algorithm to avoid it. So it’s a combination of adoption, how productive we can be in the ecosystem, and how much room there is to do something better.

r001.rationale: The response says ecosystem choice depends partly on whether the hardware offers an interesting opportunity to rethink algorithms and do something better.
